Abstract
Large Language Models are being increas-
ingly deployed as the decision-making core
of autonomous agents capable of effecting
change in external environments. Yet, in con-
versational benchmarks, which simulate real-
world customer-centric issue resolution sce-
narios, these agents frequently fail due to the
cascading effects of incorrect decision-making.
These challenges are particularly pronounced
for open-source LLMs with smaller parame-
ter sizes, limited context windows, and con-
strained inference budgets, which contribute to
increased error accumulation in agentic settings.
To tackle these challenges, we present the
Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic (FAMA) frame-
work. FAMA operates in two stages: first, it an-
alyzes failure trajectories from baseline agents
to identify the most prevalent errors; second, it
employs an orchestration mechanism that ac-
tivates a minimal subset of specialized agents
tailored to address these failures by injecting a
targeted context for the tool-use agent before
the decision-making step. Experiments across
open-source LLMs demonstrate performance
gains up to 27% across evaluation modes over
standard baselines. These results highlight that
targeted curation of context through special-
ized agents to address common failures is a
valuable design principle for building reliable,
multi-turn tool-use LLM agents that simulate
real-world conversational scenarios.

DeepMind, 2025; OpenAI, 2025) have significantly
enhanced their potential to function as the decision-
making backbone of autonomous agents (Chowa
et al., 2025). Such agents are now being tested
across a broad spectrum of applications, ranging

Prior work has largely sought to improve tool-
using agents through task-specific supervised fine-
tuning (Chen et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024), or
reinforcement learning–based optimization (Acik-
goz et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025b; Jiang et al.,
2025). For multi-turn tool-use/tool-calling tasks,
where trajectories are lengthy, partially observable,
and highly variable (Kate et al., 2025; Wang et al.,
2025b): collecting sufficient high-quality supervi-
sion or reward-aligned experience becomes pro-
hibitively expensive (Saeidi et al., 2026; Golubev
et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b). Re-
inforcement learning methods (Zhang et al., 2025b)
are not overall effective for these challenges, as
training requires large-scale curated trajectories, re-
peated execution of complex tool interactions and
long episodes to propagate sparse and delayed re-
wards, leading to substantial compute and engineer-
ing overhead (Wang et al., 2023, 2025c). Moreover,
because training objectives are typically optimized
over learning patterns of correct behavior, these
methods rarely target the specific failure patterns
exhibited by a given agent (Rauba et al., 2024), lim-
iting their effectiveness in addressing systematic
errors observed in practice.
We have also observed that there has been lim-
ited exploration (Nekoei et al., 2025; Fu et al.,
2024) of training-free improvement techniques that
extract failure signals from agent trajectories and
use them to modularly orchestrate agentic systems
built specifically on smaller open-source language
models (Belcak et al., 2025). While larger models
benefit from extensive pretraining and long context
windows, their deployment is often impractical in
real-world settings due to cost, latency, and pri-
vacy constraints (Liang and Tong, 2025). More-
over, scaling alone can mask, rather than resolve,
fundamental deficiencies in long-horizon decision-
making and tool use. Small language models ex-
pose these limitations more clearly (Shen et al.,
2024; Sinha et al., 2025), making them an ideal
testbed for studying systematic agent failures un-
der realistic resource constraints.


In this work, we argue that reliable multi-turn
tool use requires failure-aware agent composi-
tion. We introduce a two-stage framework, named
the Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic (FAMA) frame-
work, that explicitly identifies the most prevalent
failure modes in language agent conversation trajec-
tories and dynamically adapts the tool-use agent’s
internal prior context to mitigate those failures.
FAMA operates in two stages. First, it analyzes fail-
ure trajectories produced by a baseline agent and
categorizes errors into a small set of common fail-
ure types. Rather than treating all errors equally,
this analysis surfaces the dominant errors that most
strongly impact performance.
In the second stage, the FAMA framework em-
ploys a lightweight routing mechanism consisting
of an orchestrator and a mitigation agent (Figure 2)
that selectively activates a set of specialized LLM
helper-agents designed to address these specific
weaknesses (see §4.1). By dynamically construct-
ing the agent’s prior context using only the nec-
essary agents, FAMA avoids the overhead of ex-
cessive context injection while directly addressing
the agent’s most critical shortcomings (Figure 1).
This design motivates our use of the term ‘meta-
agentic’, as the proposed system does not act in the
environment directly, but operates at a higher level
by reasoning over agent behaviors, diagnosing their
failures, and dynamically composing a minimal set
of specialized agents to shape the decision-relevant
context of the underlying tool-use agent.
We evaluate FAMA across τ-bench, τ-trait and
ACEBench using a set of open-source LM back-
bones with parametric sizes ranging from 4-72 bil-
lion. Our results demonstrate consistent improve-
ments in tool-use accuracy, trajectory reliability,
and context efficiency. FAMA yields noticeable
task-success gains of up to 25% in τ-bench, 27%
in ACEBench and 24% in τ-trait over baselines
for open-source model backbones, highlighting the
effectiveness of targeted error mitigation over brute-
force context injection. In summary, our main con-
tributions are:

2
Related Works
LLM-based Tool-Use Benchmarks
While early
benchmarks primarily evaluated isolated tool calls
in response to single-turn queries (Patil et al., 2024;
Li et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023), recent work has
increasingly shifted toward multi-turn, interactive
tool-use benchmarks (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al.,
2025; Chen et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Lu et al.,
2025a; Liu et al., 2024). These benchmarks expose
long-horizon reasoning challenges for language
agents (Cemri et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2025) under
partial observability, and sustained environment
and task constraints, highlighting the need for agent
designs that explicitly address failure accumulation
over extended interaction trajectories as a valuable
direction.
Training-Free Techniques for Tool-Using Agents
A range of techniques, including structured prompt-
ing (Yao et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022), and modu-
lar agent orchestration (Mishra et al., 2025; Zhang
et al., 2025e; Zhao et al., 2025a), have been devel-
oped to improve language agents without updat-
ing model parameters. However, these approaches
are predominantly evaluated on strong or propri-
etary LLM backbones, with large context windows
and robust reasoning capabilities (Qu et al., 2025;
Chowa et al., 2025). This remains relatively under-
explored for smaller open-source models remains
comparatively, particularly in tool-use settings (Bel-
cak et al., 2025) where limited context, weaker
planning, and error accumulation pose significant
challenges (Shen et al., 2024), and training tech-
niques are dominantly explored (Jhandi et al., 2025;
Zeng et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025). FAMA attempts
to tackle these challenges by specifically focusing
on agentic design through failure modes of smaller
open-source LLM agents.
Failure-Aware Agentic Orchestration
Recent
work has begun to systematically analyze agent
failures in multi-agent LLM systems (Cemri et al.,
2025; Lu et al., 2025b), uncovering diverse fail-


ure causes (Mishra et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2025)
and proposing taxonomies and annotation datasets
to enable more principled debugging and evalu-
ation (Zhu et al., 2025; Banerjee et al., 2025).
Other efforts automate failure tracing and attribu-
tion (Zhang et al., 2025c; Ge et al., 2025) to local-
ize error sources. Although reflective (Shinn et al.,
2023; Madaan et al., 2023) and experiential (Zhang
et al., 2025d; Huang et al., 2025) feedback tech-
niques exist, and recent episodic guidance/hinting
works (Nekoei et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2024; Wang
et al., 2025d) come close in principle, they do not
leverage observed failure patterns to dynamically
compose model-specific modular agent scaffolds
under resource constraints, an angle we explore
with our FAMA framework.
3
Problem Statement
For simulating ideal testbeds of tool-use in multi-
turn conversations, we utilize tasks from bench-
marks such as τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024), τ-trait
(He et al., 2025), and ACEBench (Chen et al.,
2025a).
These benchmarks are specifically de-
signed to assess the decision-making capabilities
of language agents in realistic, multi-turn interac-
tion settings. In these setups, both the user and
the customer-service assistant are simulated by
LLMs, enabling a controlled yet dynamic envi-
ronment for analyzing interactive behavior. The
customer-service agent is the language agent that
generates the tokens signifying which tools are to
be invoked, while following the specific domain
policies. As explained in Shekkizhar et al. (2025),
the benchmarks used here do not evaluate standard
multi-agent settings (Stone and Veloso, 2000) as
the distinct agents simulating different roles, such
as the user or the assistant, can have private internal
states and competing utilities. Further details on
these benchmarks are provided in Appendix B.
4
Method
Although frontier models in agentic frameworks
demonstrate strong performance on complex, dy-
namic tasks, their deployment is often prohibitively
expensive. Additionally, integrating these models
into private or proprietary products is often imprac-
tical due to cost and security constraints. Open-
source models, by contrast, offer a viable alterna-
tive; their smaller size enables local deployment,
making them more cost-effective and better suited
for privacy-sensitive applications.
Recent works (Liu et al., 2025b; Rrv et al., 2025;
Handa et al., 2025b) show that open-source models,
along with inference-time frameworks built around
them, can achieve performance comparable to fron-
tier models on mathematical and reasoning tasks;
however, their use within agentic frameworks to
solve a complex task remains challenging. Due
to their smaller size and the nature of the data on
which they are fine-tuned, these models exhibit dis-
tinct failure modes and limitations. Additionally,
strict context constraints limit their applicability in
complex multi-agent frameworks, where multiple
agents must collaborate to solve a task, and rapidly
fill up the context windows. These factors lead
open-source models to exhibit weaker decision-
making capabilities compared to frontier models.
To address these challenges, we propose the
Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic (FAMA) frame-
work, a general and dynamic framework designed
to identify failure patterns in the behavior of open-
source model agents and determine an effective set
of agents that achieves improved performance un-
der resource constraints. In the following sections,
we present and analyze the FAMA framework in
detail.
4.1
Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic Framework
We assume the availability of a predefined set of
agents A, where each individual agent is denoted
by a ∈A, and subsets of agents are denoted by
A′ ⊆A. The full agent set A is adapted from
Mishra et al. (2025), which proposes a collection
of specialized agents for improving performance in
tool-calling environments, and is further extended
with additional modules tailored to the benchmarks
evaluated in this work. Specifically, A includes a
Domain Constraints Extractor Agent (DCE), a Tool
Suggestion Agent (TSA), a Tool Output Reformu-
lator Agent (TOR), a Planner Agent, a Decision
Verifier Agent, and a User Context Manager (Mem-
ory) module.
We further assume the availability of a prede-
fined set of general error categories representing
common agent failures, denoted by E, where a real-
ized error instance is denoted by e ∈E. Based on
prior studies (Mishra et al., 2025; Shekkizhar et al.,
2025; Kokane et al., 2024) and our own analysis,
we categorize failures in tool-calling environments
into four classes: (1) Domain Policy Violation, (2)
Incorrect Retrieval from Complex Tool Outputs,
(3) Contextual Misinterpretation and Hallucination,
and (4) Incomplete Fulfillment or Early Stopping.


Detailed definitions of these error categories are
provided in Appendix E.
Given the agent set A and the error category
set E, we define |E| independent error analysis
agents, each responsible for detecting the cause of
failure associated with a specific error category e.
These agents operate over a predefined list of fail-
ure causes derived from empirical analysis of base-
line trajectories. Additional details on the causes of
failure for each error category are provided in Ap-
pendix E. Each error analysis agent produces both
a categorical decision and a supporting rationale in
textual form.
The textual outputs and rationales produced by
all error analysis agents are concatenated into a
single input and, together with the full interaction
trajectory between the user and the tool-calling
agent for a given task τ, are passed to the orchestra-
tor agent for final failure attribution. This process
explicitly accounts for cases in which an agent may
initially make incorrect decisions but later recover
after receiving feedback from the environment, en-
suring that failure attribution reflects the overall
trajectory rather than isolated errors.
In the final stage, conditioned on the error cate-
gories identified by the orchestrator agent and the
functional definitions of agents in A, a dedicated
mitigation agent determines an efficient subset of
agents A∗⊆A that can mitigate a specific error
category e. Aggregating the mitigation agent’s rec-
ommendations across the selected error categories
yields a final agent subset that represents the mini-
mal configuration required to address the dominant
failure modes.
We collect these recommendations across tasks
and deploy multi-agent frameworks composed only
of the selected agent subsets (See Algorithm 1).
The results reported in Tables 1-4 demonstrate that
FAMA consistently achieves better performance
across different settings compared to IRMA, ReAct,
and FC on both τ-bench, τ-trait, and ACEBench
across different models.

Models.
We evaluate models from the Qwen fam-
ily, including Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B,
Qwen3-32B, and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. We ex-
clude reasoning- or thinking-augmented variants
from our study, as they fall outside the scope of this
work. Our analysis indicates that such models con-
sume a substantial portion of their token budget in
the internal reasoning process, which introduces to-
ken limit constraints when deployed within agentic
frameworks. As a result, these models tend to ex-
hibit inferior performance in tool-calling settings.
Methods.
To assess the effectiveness of FAMA,
we compare it against several established baselines,
including Function Calling (FC), ReAct, and the
Input-Reformulation Multi-Agent framework
(IRMA). The IRMA study also investigates an
enhanced variant incorporating a Self-Reflection
mechanism, and reports improved performance
over the standard IRMA setup. Since this exten-
sion is orthogonal to our focus, we do not include
it in our experiments and leave its integration with
FAMA for future work.

Conclusion
In this work, we present the Failure-Aware Meta-
Agentic (FAMA) framework, a dynamic multi-
agent approach designed to overcome the limita-
tions of open-source language agents in interactive
environments such as tool calling. FAMA operates
in two stages: first, it analyzes agent failures to
identify dominant error patterns; second, it selects
a minimal, task-relevant subset of agents via an or-
chestrator framework to mitigate these errors. We
evaluate FAMA across three interactive tool-calling
benchmarks and four open-source LLMs. Results
and analyses demonstrate the potential of FAMA as
a generalizable, failure-aware orchestration frame-
work for constructing optimized prior contexts as a
key design principle for improving and building de-
pendable, resource-efficient conversational agents.
Limitations
While the proposed Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic
(FAMA) framework achieves consistent improve-
ments across multiple benchmarks, several limita-
tions remain.
First, FAMA operates over a predefined pool of
specialized agents inherited from the underlying
agentic framework (§4.1). This design reflects a
common setting in existing user-facing, modular
tool-use systems, where a fixed set of components
is orchestrated rather than dynamically generated.
As a result, FAMA’s effectiveness is bounded by
the coverage of this agent pool: failure modes that
are not well captured by existing agents may not
be adequately mitigated. Importantly, this assump-
tion does not imply rigidity. FAMA is designed
to be extensible. New specialized agents targeting
emerging failure patterns can be incorporated with-
out modifying the orchestration mechanism. How-
ever, the current framework does not address the
automatic discovery or synthesis of such agents,
which remains an important direction for future
work.
Furthermore, the benchmarks considered in this
study primarily focus on structured conversational
environments. While these settings provide a con-
trolled testbed for analyzing failure-aware orches-
tration, they do not capture the full spectrum of in-
teractive agent deployments. Extending FAMA to
more diverse settings, including embodied, multi-
modal, or open-ended environments with less well-
defined failure taxonomies, is an important avenue
for future investigation.

B
Detail of Benchmarks
Each task in τ-bench, τ-trait and ACEBench is
formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Deci-
sion Process (POMDP) (Åström, 1965), in which
an assistant agent interacts with a user entity/agent
through a sequence of natural language conversa-
tions and tool invocations. At each step, the agent
must decide which function calls to issue based on
the current conversational context and partial ob-
servations derived from the external environment.
Executed function calls produce structured outputs
that are incorporated into the evolving dialogue
and inform subsequent decisions. This interaction
proceeds over multiple turns until task termination,
at which point the agent is evaluated using the ap-
propriate benchmark-prescribed metric centered
around successful conversation/task completion.
τ-bench
τ-bench evaluates tool using conver-
sational agents in two real-world-style customer-
service domains—retail and airline, where an agent
must interact with a simulated user, follow domain
policy rules, and use API tools to update/query a
realistic backend state. In retail, the benchmark in-
cludes a database with 500 users, 50 products, and
1,000 orders, exposes 15 tools total (7 write + 8 non-
write), and provides 115 tasks spanning actions like
cancellations, returns/exchanges, address changes,
and information requests; in airline, it includes 500
users, 300 flights, and 2,000 reservations, has 13
tools (6 write + 7 non-write), and contains 50 tasks
around booking/modifying/canceling reservations
and refund-related workflows.
τ-trait

of τ-bench that keeps the multi-turn tool-use set-
ting but adds persona-aware user simulation and

C
Analysis of the τ-trait Results
To demonstrate the generalizability of the FAMA
framework, we evaluate it on τ-trait, which in-
cludes four domains: Retail, Airline, Telehealth,
and Telecom. Since we have already analyzed per-
formance on the Airline and Retail domains in τ-
bench, we focus our evaluation on the Telehealth
and Telecom domains.
Similar to τ-bench, Domain Constraint Vio-
lations (DCV) and Contextual Misinterpretation
(CM) are identified as critical error sources by the
orchestrator agent, as shown in Figure 12. How-
ever, unlike Tau-Bench, memory-related issues are
more prominent across Tau-Trait domains, with


Incomplete Fulfillment (IFU) emerging as the pri-
mary cause of task failures. As illustrated in Figure
13, the mitigation agent frequently recommends
the Memory module for a larger number of mod-
els. Consequently, using only the Memory module
significantly improves the performance of open-
source models and, in some cases, yields better
results than combinations that also include the Do-
main Constraints Extractor (DCE) agent.
The results in Table 4 show that FAMA con-
sistently outperforms IRMA across both the Tele-
com and Telehealth domains on pass^k, for k =
1, . . . , 5. While certain methods, such as FC, out-
perform FAMA in isolated cases, FC does not
demonstrate consistent performance across do-
mains and exhibits substantial variability depend-
ing on the domain and model. These results further
highlight the robustness and generalizability of the
FAMA framework across diverse settings.
D
Analysis of the ACEBench Results
ACEBench is another benchmark used to evalu-
ate the FAMA framework. Although ACEBench
supports multiple evaluation settings, we focus on
the multi-turn agent configuration, where an active
user agent interacts with a tool-calling agent. We
compare FAMA against the Base Agent defined in
ACEBench and the ReAct framework.
The results in Figure 14 illustrate the distribu-
tion of failure causes on ACEBench as identified
by the orchestrator agent. As shown in the fig-
ure, all evaluated models suffer from significant
Contextual Misinterpretation (CM) issues, mani-
fested as incomplete task execution, misinterpreta-
tion during problem solving, and incorrect interac-
tions with the environment. To address these issues,
the mitigation agent consistently recommends the
inclusion of Planner and Verifier agents, which are
well-suited to correcting such failures as shown in
Figure 15.
The results reported in Table 3 show that aug-
menting ReAct and the Base Agent with FAMA
leads to consistent performance improvements over
other baselines, even with the addition of only
two auxiliary agents.

E
Error Categories and Causes of the
Failures
In this section, we first describe the error categories
and then elaborate on the underlying causes of fail-
ure associated with each category. The definition
of each error category is provided below.
Domain Policy Violation:
This error refers to
a failure mode in which a tool-using agent issues
an action or tool invocation that contravenes the
explicit operational rules, constraints, or policies of
the simulated domain defined by the environment.
These policies govern which actions are permissi-
ble under specific states and preconditions. A vio-
lation occurs when the agent ignores, misinterprets,
or incorrectly applies these domain rules, such as
invoking a return operation that is disallowed by
the retail domain’s return policy in τ-bench, re-
sulting in an invalid state transition. Because the
environment enforces domain policies strictly, such
violations cause the task execution trajectory to ter-
minate unsuccessfully, even if the agent’s intent
aligns with the high-level task objective.
Incorrect Retrieval from Complex Tool Outputs:
refers to a failure mode in which a tool-using agent
fails to correctly extract relevant information from
prior tool responses stored in its context. This error
typically arises when tool outputs are large, un-
structured, or weakly structured (e.g., verbose logs,
nested text fields, or mixed natural language and
metadata), making it difficult for the agent to re-
liably identify the correct entities, values, or state
variables required for subsequent actions. As a re-
sult, the agent conditions later tool calls or reason-
ing steps on incorrect or incomplete information,
leading to invalid decisions or task failure despite
the necessary information being present in the en-
vironment output.
Contextual Misinterpretation and Hallucina-
tion:
refers to a failure mode in which a tool-
using agent incorrectly infers the user’s underlying
intent due to nuanced, ambiguous, or adversarial
natural language instructions. Instead of grounding
its interpretation in the domain’s available oper-
ations and constraints, the agent over-literalizes
phrasing, overlooks implied intent, or hallucinates
an incorrect task formulation. This results in the
selection and invocation of an inappropriate tool,
such as executing a return operation when the user
implicitly intends an exchange, despite the correct
intent being inferable from contextual or domain
knowledge.
Incomplete Fulfillment or Early Stopping:
refers to a failure mode in which a tool-using agent
does not fully satisfy all components of the user’s
task requirements before terminating or effectively
abandoning the interaction. This error commonly
arises in long-horizon, multi-turn trajectories where
the agent must track multiple obligations across
conversational turns while operating over large,
unstructured tool outputs. As the interaction pro-
gresses, the agent may lose track of pending sub-
goals, become over-focused on intermediate tool
calls, or prematurely conclude the task, resulting in
unmet user requests despite partial progress.
To enable judgment agents to detect task fail-
ures, a detailed list of failure causes is required.
Accordingly, we analyze the trajectories produced
by baseline methods and provide a comprehensive
list of failure causes for each error category, as
described below.
Cause of Domain Policy Violation
1. The assistant performs an action that the policy
explicitly forbids
2. The assistant skips a step that the policy explicitly
requires
3. The assistant proceeds without meeting conditions
the policy requires
4. The assistant makes commitments that contradict
policy rules
5. The assistant uses data/arguments not provided by
user or tools (fabrication)
Cause of Wrong Retrieval from Complex
Tool Outputs
1. The agent states information that differs from what
the tool output actually contains
2. The agent miscounts items or provides wrong
totals from tool outputs
3. The agent selects wrong items when correct op-
tions exist in tool output
4. The agent misses relevant data in tool output that
would change the action
5. The agent attributes data to the wrong entity when


multiple exist in output
6. The agent uses wrong values (IDs, prices, dates,
etc.) from tool output
Cause of Incomplete Fulfillment or Early
Stopping
The user may have multiple requirements, questions,
or actions they need completed. This error occurs
when the agent:
1. Addresses only some parts of a multi-part request
2. Stops after encountering a difficulty without trying
alternatives
3. Receives confirmation to proceed but never exe-
cutes the action
4. Terminates the conversation with unfinished tasks
Cause of Contextual Misinterpretation
and Hallucination
The user’s request may have specific intent, context,
or nuances that the agent must correctly understand
to take appropriate actions. This error occurs when
the agent:
1. Understands the words but misses the actual intent
2. Confuses which entity/item/order the user is refer-
ring to
3. Misapplies criteria or constraints the user specified
4. Takes an action that doesn’t match what the user
actually wanted

Abstract: Large Language Models are being increas- ingly deployed as the decision-making core of autonomous agents capable of effecting change in external environments. Yet, in con- versational benchmarks, which simulate real- world customer-centric issue resolution sce- narios, these agents frequently fail due to the cascading effects of incorrect decision-making. These challenges are particularly pronounced for open-source LLMs with smaller parame- ter sizes, limited context windows, and con- strained inference budgets, which contribute to increased error accumulation in agentic settings. To tackle these challenges, we present the Failure-Aware Meta-Agentic (FAMA) frame- work. FAMA operates in two stages: first, it an- alyzes failure trajectories from baseline agents to identify the most prevalent errors; second, it employs an orchestration mechanism that ac- tivates a minimal subset of specialized agents tailored to address these failures by injecting a targeted context for the tool-use agent before the decision-making step. Experiments across open-source LLMs demonstrate performance gains up to 27% across evaluation modes over standard baselines. These results highlight that targeted curation of context through special- ized agents to address common failures is a valuable design principle for building reliable, multi-turn tool-use LLM agents that simulate real-world conversational scenarios.
